rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb’s wife said he remained motionless, bent over, and crying day and night after the affair.
rows.anchor: والله ما به حركة لشيء ما زال مكبا يبكي الليل والنهار

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: After fifty nights of the boycott, Kaʿb prayed at dawn on his roof, heard a herald from Mount Salʿ announce relief, and fell prostrate.
rows.anchor: فلما مضت خمسون ليلة من حين نهى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن كلامنا

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: The herald’s voice reached Kaʿb before the mounted messenger; Kaʿb gave him his clothes and borrowed garments to wear.
rows.anchor: وكان الصوت أسرع من فرسه

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: The repentance revelation came late at night; Umm Salama urged the Prophet to announce it, and Talha alone among the Emigrants hurried to greet Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: وكانت توبتنا نزلت على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلثي الليل

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb asked whether his acceptance came from God or the Prophet; the Prophet answered that it came from God and recited the passage about God turning to the Prophet and Emigrants.
rows.anchor: قال: «بل من عند الله»

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb vowed to give all his wealth in charity as repentance, but the Prophet advised him to keep some, so he retained his share from Khaybar.
rows.anchor: أمسك عليك بعض مالك فهو أخير لك

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb considered God’s blessing of truthful testimony greater than any post-Islam blessing and hoped to remain truthful; he says he had not lied since.
rows.anchor: ما تعمدت كذبة منذ قلت ذلك لرسول الله إلى يومي هذا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators explain that the whole earth became constricted and their own selves felt tight from anxiety and loneliness.
rows.anchor: ضاقت صدورهم بالهم والوحشة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq defines sincere repentance as the constriction felt by Kaʿb and his companions even though the earth was spacious.
rows.anchor: أن تضيق علينا بما رحبت ويضيق عليه نفسه كتوبة كعب وصاحبه

rows.speaker: أبو يزيد
rows.claim: Abu Yazid says he mistakenly thought he loved God, pleased Him, remembered Him, and repented, then learned God had first loved, approved, remembered, and accepted him.
rows.anchor: وشئت أن أتوب فإذا هو تاب علي

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafiʿ explains being with the truthful as being with Muhammad and his Companions.
rows.anchor: قال نافع: يعني مع محمد وأصحابه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr identifies the truthful as Abu Bakr and Umar.
rows.anchor: سعيد بن جبير: مع أبي بكر وعمر

rows.speaker: ابن جريج وابن حبان
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Hibban identify the truthful as the Emigrants, citing the description of the poor Emigrants as truthful.
rows.anchor: ابن جريح وابن حبان: مع المهاجرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih, says the truthful are Ali ibn Abi Talib and his companions.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في هذه الآية يا أيها الذين آمنوا اتقوا الله وكونوا مع الصادقين قال:

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar, through Jabir, says the truthful are the Family of Muhammad.
rows.anchor: عن جابر عن أبي جعفر في قوله تعالى وكونوا مع الصادقين قال:

rows.speaker: يمان بن رباب
rows.claim: Yaman ibn Rabab urges believers to be truthful as the three men who stayed behind were truthful.
rows.anchor: يمان بن رباب: أصدقوا كما صدق الثلاثة الذين خلفوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says believers should join those whose intentions, hearts, and deeds were true and who sincerely went with the Prophet to Tabuk.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: مع الذين صدقت نياتهم فاستقامت قلوبهم وأعمالهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada takes truthfulness to mean sincerity of intention and truth in private and public, night and day.
rows.anchor: قتادة: يعني الصدق في النية

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reportedly recited the command as be with the truthful, emphasizing the imperative to accompany them.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن مسعود يقول: كونوا مع! الصادقين وكذا كان يقرأها

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from Abdullah says lying is forbidden in seriousness and jest, including promising children something and failing to fulfill it.
rows.anchor: إن الكذب لا يصلح منه جد ولا هزل ولا أن يعد أحدكم صبيته شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that it was not for Medina’s people has the form of a report but means a prohibition.
rows.anchor: ما كان لأهل المدينة ظاهره خبر معناه نهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surrounding desert tribes, including Muzayna, Juhayna, Aslam, and Ghifar, must not stay behind from the Messenger’s campaigns or prefer themselves over him.
rows.anchor: ومن حولهم من الأعراب سكان البوادي مزينة وجهينة وأسجح وأسلم وغفار أن يتخلفوا عن رسول الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains that the believers should not spare themselves the same hardships that the Messenger endures on campaign.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: يعني لا يرغبون بأنفسهم أن تصيبهم من الشدائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thirst, fatigue, hunger, enemy-provoking steps, and any gain from an enemy—killing, capture, or booty—are recorded as righteous deeds.
rows.anchor: ذلك بأنهم لا يصيبهم في سفرهم ظمأ عطش، وقرأ عبد بن عمير ظماء بالمد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says each fright suffered in God’s path earns seventy thousand good deeds; the report also promises heavenly drink and relief from fatigue.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: بكل روعة تنالهم في سبيل الله سبعين ألف حسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every bodily part and every posture or movement in God’s path is granted testimony and intercession.
rows.anchor: ومن خرج في سبيل الله لم يضع قدما ولا يدا ولا جنبا ولا أنفا ولا ركبة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the command specially concerns a campaign led personally by the Prophet, when no one may stay behind unless Muslims need them elsewhere.
rows.anchor: فقال قتادة: وهذه خاصة لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا غزا بنفسه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said he would never stay behind a campaign if not for hardship on his community and lack of means to take everyone with him.
rows.anchor: لولا أن أشق على أمتي ما تخلفت خلف سرية يغزو في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي وابن المبارك والفزاري وابن جابر وسعيد بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: These scholars say the verse applies to the first and last generations of the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: يقولون في هذه الآية: إنها لأول هذه الأمة وآخرها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the strict rule applied when Muslims were few and was abrogated when 9:122 allowed some believers to remain behind for instruction.
rows.anchor: هذا حين كان أهل الإسلام قليلا فلما كثروا نسخها الله وأباح التخلف لمن شاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every small or large expense and every valley crossed on the march is recorded, including the tracks left behind, for full reward and entry to Paradise without reckoning.
rows.anchor: ولا ينفقون في سبيل الله نفقة صغيرة ولا كبيرة ولو علاقة سوط

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report from several Companions says each dirham sent to support a fighter who stays home earns seven hundred, while a fighter’s dirham earns seven hundred thousand; it cites God’s multiplication of reward.
rows.anchor: ومن أرسل نفقة في سبيل الله وأقام في بيته فله بكل درهم سبعمائة درهم

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd interprets the storm prayer’s phrase as Ya Hayyu Ya Qayyum: if God saves them from the violent wind, they will be grateful through faith and obedience.
rows.anchor: أهيا شراهيا وتفسيره: يا حي يا قيوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After rescue, people transgress unjustly, but the burden and consequence of their wrongdoing return to themselves.
rows.anchor: فلما أنجاهم إذا هم يبغون يظلمون ويتجاوزون إلى غير أمر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis ends the sentence after the preceding clause; another joins it, taking transgression as subject and worldly enjoyment as its predicate, which cannot serve as provision for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: والبغي ابتداء ومتاع خبره، وقوله على أنفسكم صلة المتاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq and Hafs read mutāʿan in the accusative as a circumstantial expression.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن إسحاق وحفص: متاعا بالنصب على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly life is like rain that mingles with earth’s plants: people eat grains, vegetables, and fruits, while livestock graze on herbage.
rows.anchor: كماء أنزلناه من السماء فاختلط به نبات الأرض مما يأكل الناس من الحبوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading is wa-zzayyanat; Ibn Masʿud’s reading wa-tazayyanat confirms the sense that the earth becomes adorned.
rows.anchor: وازينت هذا قراءة العامة، وتصديقها قراءة عبد الله بن مسعود: وتزينت

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان النهدي والضحاك
rows.claim: Abu Uthman al-Nahdi and al-Dahhak read wāzānat on the pattern of ajāzat; ʿAwf says their elders read it likewise.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عثمان النهدي والضحاك: وازانت على وزن اجازت

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء وأبو العالية والشعبي والحسن والأعرج
rows.claim: These readers pronounce wa-zzayyanat with a separated hamza and light form; Qutrub glosses it as bringing forth its adornment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء وأبو العالية والشعبي والحسن والأعرج: وازينت على وزن أفعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse says the earth thinks it can control its produce, the pronoun is explained as the plants, the harvest, or the adornment.
rows.anchor: أخبر عن الأرض ويعني للنبات إذ كان مفهوما وقيل: رده إلى الغلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s command means His decree of destruction; ḥaṣīd describes crops cut down and uprooted.
rows.anchor: أتاها أمرنا قضاؤنا بهلاكها ليلا أو نهارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ka-an lam taghn means the land had not remained inhabited; its root refers to a place where someone stayed and built.
rows.anchor: كأن لم تغن تكن، وأصله من غني المكان إذا أقام فيه وعمره،

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The common reading has feminine taghn referring to the earth, while Qatada reads yaghn with the masculine referent al-zukhruf.
rows.anchor: وقرأها العامة: تغن بالتاء لتأنيث الأرض، وقرأها قتادة بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poetic line uses salāma as safety, helping explain the name Abode of Peace.
rows.anchor: تحيى بالسلامة أم بكر … وهل لك بعد رهطك من سلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is called the Abode of Peace because those who enter are safe from afflictions, as another verse welcomes them in peace and safety.
rows.anchor: فسميت الجنة دار السلام لأن من دخلها سلم من الآفات

rows.speaker: ذو النون المصري
rows.claim: Dhu al-Nun says Paradise bears this name because its inhabitants are safe from separation and severance.
rows.anchor: وقال ذو النون المصري: سميت بذلك لأن من دخلها سلم من القطيعة والفراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes salām as greeting: Paradise’s inhabitants greet one another and angels greet them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد به التحية يقال: سلم تسليما وسلاما كما يقال: كلم تكليما

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says greeting never ceases among Paradise’s inhabitants and is their salutation.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: السلام لا ينقطع عن أهل الجنة وهو تحيتهم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq says God Himself greets Paradise’s inhabitants first, comforting them about remembered sins and awe of the Knower of hidden things.
rows.anchor: سميت بذلك لأن من دخلها سلم عليه المولى وذلك أن الله يعلم ما فيه أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: In a dream parable narrated by Jabir, God is the king, Islam the house, Paradise its inner room and banquet, and Muhammad the messenger; those who answer him enter and eat there.
rows.anchor: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يوما فقال: «إني رأيت في المنام كأن جبرائيل

rows.speaker: يحيى بن معاذ
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Muʿadh warns that answering God’s invitation from worldly life admits one to the Abode of Peace, while answering from the grave bars one from it.
rows.anchor: يا ابن آدم دعاك الله إلى دار السلام فانظر من أين تجيبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The invitation to the Abode of Peace is universal to establish God’s proof, whereas guidance on the straight path is specially granted.
rows.anchor: عم بالدعوة إظهارا لحجته وخص بالهداية استغناء عن خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative says the call to the Abode of Peace is general because it is the route to blessing, while guidance to the straight path is specific because it leads to the Benefactor.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الدعوة إلى الدار عامة لأنها الطريق إلى النعمة وهداية الصراط خاصة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda takes am as wāw, reading the accusation as and they say Muhammad invented the Quran himself.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: أم بمعنى الواو أي ويقولون افتراه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge is to produce a surah resembling the Quran; Ibn al-Sumayqi reads the phrase with an annexation, whose pronoun may refer to the Quran or the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن السميقع: بسورة مثله مضافة، فتحتمل أن تكون الهاء كناية عن القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan explains the challenge to call on whomever they can to help oppose the Quran.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن كيسان: وادعوا من استطعتم على المخالفة ليعينوكم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets witnesses as people who can testify in support of the claim that Muhammad fabricated the Quran.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: شهداءكم بمعنى ناسا يشهدون لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers rejected the Quran before comprehending it and before its promised outcome had arrived.
rows.anchor: بل كذبوا بما لم يحيطوا بعلمه يعني القرآن ولما يأتهم تأويله تفسيره

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says taʾwīl here is the Quran’s consequence, what God promised would happen; it means the eventual outcome of events.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: يعني عاقبته وما وعد الله في القرآن

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Husayn ibn al-Fadl locates the saying that people oppose what they do not know in two Quran passages, including 10:39 and 46:11.
rows.anchor: وقيل للحسين بن الفضل: هل تجد في القرآن (من جهل شيئا عاداه؟) فقال: نعم في موضعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier unbelieving nations also denied revelation, and the passage warns the current deniers by pointing to the destruction of former wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: كذلك كذب الذين من قبلهم من كفار الأمم الخالية فانظر كيف كان عاقبة الظالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some of Muhammad’s people will believe and some will not, as God already knows; He knows those who will corrupt.
rows.anchor: وربك أعلم بالمفسدين الذين لا يؤمنون

rows.speaker: مجاهد ومقاتل
rows.claim: Mujahid and Muqatil say the declaration that each side owns its own deed and is disavowed by the other was abrogated by the jihad verse.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل والكلبي: هذه الآية منسوخة بآية الجهاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who hear and see outwardly still fail to benefit from Quranic signs; as the Prophet cannot create hearing or sight, he cannot grant faith to those God has decreed will not believe.
rows.anchor: ما لا تقدر أن تسمع من سلبته السمع، ولا تقدر أن تخلق للأعمى بصرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not wrong people in any act, because He is just in all His actions.
rows.anchor: إن الله لا يظلم الناس شيئا لأنه في جميع أفعاله عادل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People wrong themselves through disbelief, sin, and doing what they have no right to do.
rows.anchor: ولكن الناس أنفسهم يظلمون بالكفر والمعصية وفعلهم ما ليس لهم أن يفعلوا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the gathered people will feel they remained in worldly life only an hour because its duration shrinks before the terrors ahead.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: كأن لم يلبثوا في الدنيا إلا ساعة من النهار قصرت الدنيا في أعينهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they seem to have stayed in their graves an hour; on resurrection they recognize one another as in life, then recognition ends when they see the terrors.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كأن لم يلبثوا في قبورهم إلا قدر ساعة من النهار يتعارفون بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who denied meeting God have lost and were not guided.
rows.anchor: قد خسر الذين كذبوا بلقاء الله وما كانوا مهتدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether the Prophet sees some promised punishment in his lifetime or dies first, everyone returns to God, who witnesses and requites their deeds.
rows.anchor: فإلينا مرجعهم في الآخرة ثم الله شهيد على ما يفعلون مجزيهم به

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators identify the punishment shown before the Prophet’s death with Badr, while the rest comes after death.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: فكان البعض الذي أراه قبلهم ببدر وسائر العذاب بعد موتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every former community had a messenger; when the messenger came and they denied, God judged justly by punishing and destroying them.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاء رسولهم فكذبوه قضي بينهم بالقسط أي عذبوا في الدنيا واهلكوا

rows.speaker: مجاهد ومقاتل
rows.claim: Mujahid and Muqatil instead say the messenger arrives on the Day of Resurrection and is judged fairly against his people.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد ومقاتل: فإذا جاء رسولهم يوم القيامة قضي بينه وبينهم بالقسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God neither punishes without guilt or proof nor reduces good deeds or adds to bad deeds.
rows.anchor: لا يعذبون بغير ذنب ولا يؤاخذون بغير حجة ولا ينقصون من حسناتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers ask when the promised punishment will come; another view takes the question as asking when the Hour will arrive.
rows.anchor: ويقولون أي المشركون متى هذا الوعد الذي وعدتنا يا محمد من العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet controls neither harm nor benefit for himself except by God’s will; each community has a fixed lifespan, neither delayed nor advanced by an hour.
rows.anchor: لا أقدر لها على ضر ولا نفع إلا ما شاء الله أن أملكه لكل أمة أجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If punishment reaches them by night or day, criminals should not ask to hasten what they will already face.
rows.anchor: إن أتاكم عذابه الله بياتا ليلا أو نهارا ماذا يستعجل منه المجرمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When punishment arrives, the unbelievers are asked whether they now believe in it, although they had previously demanded it and denied it.
rows.anchor: إذا ما وقع نزل العذاب آمنتم به صدقتم بالعذاب في وقت نزوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoers are told to taste enduring punishment as repayment for what they did in worldly life.
rows.anchor: ذوقوا عذاب الخلد هل تجزون اليوم إلا بما كنتم تكسبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses had announced that God might destroy the enemy and install Israel in the land, then test how they acted; he also declared that his Lord was with him and would guide him.
rows.anchor: عسى ربكم أن يهلك عدوكم ويستخلفكم في الأرض فينظر كيف تعملون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God first told Moses to strike the sea; when it did not split, He instructed him to command it to part by God’s permission, and it opened into twelve dry routes divided by raised walls.
rows.anchor: فأوحى الله تعالى إلى موسى أن كنه وقل: انفلق أبا خالد بإذن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites could not see or hear across the paths and feared their relatives had drowned, so God made the water barriers perforated for them to see one another.
rows.anchor: فأوحى الله تعالى إلى الجبال من الماء تشبكي فتشبكت وصارت فيه شبه الخروق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh hesitated at the sea; Gabriel rode a mare and Michael drove the army, and Pharaoh’s stallion followed Gabriel’s scent into the water before it closed over the troops.
rows.anchor: فلما شم أدهم فرعون ريح فرس جبرئيل، وفرعون لا يراه انسل خلف فرس جبريل

rows.speaker: جبريل
rows.claim: As Pharaoh drowned and professed belief in Israel’s God, Gabriel put sea mud into his mouth, and the Quran rebuked his late faith.
rows.anchor: فدس جبرئيل في فيه من حمأة البحر، وقال: آلآن وقد عصيت قبل

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq says God had ordered Moses and Aaron to speak gently to Pharaoh, whose eventual remembrance and fear came too late to help.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الوراق: قال الله لموسى وهارون: فقولا له قولا لينا لعله يتذكر

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb relates that after the Nile stopped, Pharaoh privately prostrated and pleaded for water; Gabriel came as a petitioner asking how a servant’s betrayal should be punished, and Pharaoh wrote that he should drown.
rows.anchor: قال كعب: لما أمسك نيل مصر عن الجري قالت القبط لفرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Israel doubted Pharaoh had died, God cast his short red body ashore so they could see it; al-Hasan reads the verb with another dialect form.
rows.anchor: فأمر الله تعالى بالبحر فألقى فرعون على الساحل أحمر قصير كأنه ثور

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads wajawz-nā in place of the common form, and the source says both are dialect variants.
rows.anchor: البحر حتى جازوه، وقرأ الحسن [وجوزنا، وهما لغتان]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Atbaʿah means Pharaoh caught up with them; tabaʿahu or atbaʿahu can mean reaching and overtaking, while the intensified form means following behind or imitating.
rows.anchor: يقال: تبعه وأتبعه إذا أدركه ولحقه، واتبعه بالتشديد إذا سار خلفه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads ʿuduwan with a rounded first vowel and doubled wāw; the commentators say the accompanying terms mean verbal injustice and actional aggression.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن (عدوا) بضم العين وتشديد الواو مثل

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators distinguish baghyan as wrongdoing in speech and ʿadwan as aggression in action.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: بغيا في القول وعدوا في الفعل

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Khalaf read innahu with kasra, meaning Pharaoh professed belief and said that Israel’s God is the only deity.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف إنه بالكسر أي آمنت وقلت: إنه

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد وأبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer the other reading, anna with fatḥa, because the clause is the object of his belief statement.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الآخرون: أن بالفتح لوقوع آمنت عليها، وهي اختيار أبو عبيد وأبي حاتم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet reports Gabriel hated Iblis and Pharaoh most among jinn and humans; Gabriel says he put mud in Pharaoh’s mouth lest mercy reach him.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «قال لي جبرئيل: ما أبغضت أحدا من عباد الله إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By his body means his lifeless corpse, raised onto a high shore; the word is connected to najwah, raised ground, and a line by Aws ibn Hajar supports that meaning.
rows.anchor: قال أوس بن حجر: فمن بعقوته كمن بنجوته

rows.speaker: مجاهد والكسائي
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Kisaʾi interpret badan here as Pharaoh’s armor, since he was armored.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والكسائي: البدن هاهنا الدرع وكان دارعا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reads the phrase as casting Pharaoh onto the side of the sea; another gloss says the intended sign was his hair.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله: فاليوم ننجيك ببدنك، أي نلقيك على ناحية البحر

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali reads khalqik with qaf, making Pharaoh a sign to his Creator.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي بن أبي طالب (رضي الله عنه) : لمن خلقك [بالقاف]

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the punishment hovered above the people of Nineveh at a distance of one mile.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: كان العذاب فوق رؤوسهم قدر ميل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas estimates the looming punishment at two-thirds of a mile.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: قدر ثلثي ميل

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb describes a black cloud and smoke covering Nineveh; the people put on sackcloth, separated mothers from young, lamented, confessed belief in Jonah, and God lifted the punishment on Ashura.
rows.anchor: فلما رأوا ذلك أيقنوا بالهلاك فطلبوا نبيهم فلم يجدوه، فقذف الله في قلوبهم التوبة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud says Nineveh’s repentance included restoring wrongs, even removing a stone from a foundation and returning it to its owner.
rows.anchor: بلغ من توبة أهل نينوى أن ترادوا المظالم بينهم حتى أن كان الرجل ليأتي الحجر

rows.speaker: أبو الجلد
rows.claim: A report through Abu ʿImran says an elderly scholar taught Jonah’s people an invocation to the Living God and the punishment was lifted.
rows.anchor: فقال: قولوا: يا حي حين لا حي ويا حي [يا] محيي الموتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah left expecting his people’s destruction, feared they would call him a liar after reprieve, boarded a stuck ship, lost three lots, and was swallowed by a whale.
rows.anchor: فانطلق عاتبا على ربه، مغاضبا لقومه فأتى البحر [فإذ سفينة قد شحنت]

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the preceding group as Muhammad’s Companions.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: عنى به أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that the Quran was revealed with God’s knowledge and that there is no god but Him ends with a question whose force is a command to submit.
rows.anchor: فاعلموا أنما أنزل بعلم الله يعني القرآن وأن لا إله إلا هو فهل أنتم مسلمون لفظه استفهام ومعناه أمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who seek worldly life and its adornment through their deeds are repaid fully in this life, without shortfall.
rows.anchor: من كان يريد بعمله الحياة الدنيا وزينتها نوف إليهم أعمالهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says a person whose aim, joy, desire, and intention are worldly receives the reward of good deeds here but has none left to repay in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: من كانت الدنيا همه وقصده وسروره وطلبته ونيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A believer may receive good deeds’ rewards in both worlds, unlike the person whose worldly aim exhausts the reward in this life.
rows.anchor: وأما المؤمن فيجازى بحسناته في الدنيا ويثاب عليها في الآخرة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says whoever does good for someone receives their reward from God in both the immediate world and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: من أحسن من محسن فقد وقع أجره على الله في عاجل الدنيا وآجل الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One disagreement says the verse concerns unbelievers; believers intend both worlds, with their intention for the Hereafter prevailing, as the next verse indicates.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: هي للكفار، وأما المؤمن فإنه يريد الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies those whose deeds are void and whose only Hereafter recompense is Fire as usurers.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: هم أهل الربا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra transmits that on Judgment Day the first people summoned include a Quran reciter, a wealthy man, and one killed in battle, each questioned about what he did with his gifts.
rows.anchor: قال: ماذا عملت فيما علمت؟ قال: كنت أقوم به آناء الليل

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The reciter, donor, and fighter are each condemned as seeking fame rather than God; the Prophet says these three are the first fuel for Hell.
rows.anchor: بل أردت أن يقال فلان جريء، فقد قيل ذلك» ثم ضرب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على ركبتي فقال: «يا أبا هريرة أولئك الثلاثة

rows.speaker: معاوية
rows.claim: When Shuqayy related Abu Hurayra’s report, Muʿawiya feared what this meant for others, wept, and affirmed the verse about worldly seekers’ ruined deeds.
rows.anchor: فكيف بمن بقي من الناس؟ ثم بكى معاوية [وضرب خديه] حتى ظننا أنه هالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their apparent good works are ruined in this life and false in what they were doing.
rows.anchor: نوف إليهم أعمالهم فيها وقرأ إلى قوله: باطل ما كانوا يعملون

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators take the generations blessed with Noah’s companions to mean descendants, including saved believers, while other descendants receive worldly enjoyment and later punishment.
rows.anchor: معناه وعلى قرون تجيء من ذرية من معك من الذين آمنوا معك من ولدك

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi says the promised peace includes every believer, male and female, until the Resurrection, and the threat likewise includes every unbeliever.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن كعب القرضي: داخل في ذلك السلام كل مؤمن ومؤمنة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak rejects the claim that drowned children were punished with their parents: children died at their appointed terms, while the named adults were punished and destined for the Fire.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: زعم أناس إن من غرق من الولدان مع آبائهن وإنما ليس كذلك

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the good deeds that erase sins with the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: إن الحسنات يذهبن السيئات يعني: إن الصلوات الخمس يذهبن الخطيئات

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the good deeds are saying glorification, praise, the testimony of divine unity, and God’s greatness.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هي قول العبد: سبحان الله والحمد لله ولا إله إلا الله والله أكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was revealed about Abu al-Yusr, a date seller who embraced and kissed a woman he had lured home, stopped when she reminded him of God, then confessed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: نزلت هذه الآية في أبي اليسر عمرو بن غزية الأنصاري وكان يبيع التمر

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: After Gabriel brought the verse following the afternoon prayer, the Prophet told Abu al-Yusr that the prayer expiated his act; when Umar asked if this applied only to him, the Prophet said it applied to everyone.
rows.anchor: قال: «أشهدت معنا هذه الصلاة؟» قال: نعم، قال: «اذهب فإنها كفارة لما عملت»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase that follows may point back to what was just mentioned, or alternatively to the Quran as a reminder for those who remember.
rows.anchor: ذلك الذي ذكرناه، وقيل: هو إشارة إلى القرآن ذكرى عظة للذاكرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to endure the harm he meets; alternative explanations specify patience through harm or in prayer, as in the command to enjoin prayer on one’s family.
rows.anchor: واصبر يا محمد على ما تلقى من الأذى، وقيل: على الأذى، وقيل: على الصلاة، نظير قوله وأمر أهلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains those whose reward God does not waste as people who pray.
rows.anchor: وقال فيه ابن عباس: يعني المصلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the women’s declaration mā hādhā basharan, basharan is accusative after an omitted preposition and serves as the predicate of negative mā.
rows.anchor: ما هذا بشرا نصب بنزع حرف الصفة وعلى خبر ما الجحد

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads bashar in the nominative, a dialect of Najd; al-Farra cites poetry using the same construction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: ما هذا بشر بالرفع وهي لغة أهل نجد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra cites a second poem to show the construction used in the phrase that these two are not equal.
rows.anchor: لشتان ما أنوي وينوي بنو أبي

rows.speaker: أبو الحويرث الحنفي
rows.claim: Abu al-Huwayrith reads bashari, which al-Farra explains as buyer, yielding the sense that Joseph is no human but a noble angel.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الحويرث الحنفي أنه قرأ: ما هذا بشري، قال الفراء: يعني بمشتري

rows.speaker: ابن فورك
rows.claim: Ibn Furak says the women called Joseph a noble angel because he resisted desire and worldly adornment, contrary to ordinary human nature.
rows.anchor: إنما قلن له ملك كريم لأنه خالف ميوله وأعرض عن الدنيا وزينتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife tells the women that this is the man whose love they blamed her for, admits seducing him, and says he resisted; she threatens prison and humiliation if he disobeys.
rows.anchor: ولقد راودته عن نفسه فاستعصم أي امتنع واستعصى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic nūn in the threat is heavy in the first verb and light in the second; at pause the light nūn is written with alif, as in another Quran phrase and al-Aʿsha’s verse.
rows.anchor: والوقف على قوله: ليسجنن بالنون لكنها مشددة. وعلى قوله: وليكونا بالألف لأنها مخففة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When she persists and threatens him, Joseph prefers prison to sin and addresses God with a vocative attached to the divine name.
rows.anchor: السجن على المعصية، قال رب: يا رب، منادى مضاف

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: The common reading has al-sijn with kasra as a noun; Yaʿqub reads it with fatḥa as a verbal noun meaning imprisonment.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة بكسر السين على الاسم وقرأ يعقوب برفع السين على المصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says he may incline toward the women unless God turns their plot away; ṣabā means to lean and long for something.
rows.anchor: أصب أمل إليهن وأبايعهن، فقال صبا فلان إلى كذا

rows.speaker: يزيد بن ضبة
rows.claim: Yazid ibn Dabba’s line about his heart inclining toward Hind serves as evidence for the meaning of ṣabā.
rows.anchor: قال يزيد بن ضبة

rows.speaker: يزيد بن ضبة
rows.claim: Yazid ibn Dabba’s verse that his heart inclined toward Hind illustrates ṣabā as longing or inclination.
rows.anchor: إلى هند صبا قلبي … وهند مثلها يصبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answered Joseph’s prayer by averting their plot, for He hears his plea and knows their guile.
rows.anchor: فاستجاب له ربه فصرف عنه كيدهن إنه هو السميع لدعائه وشكايته، العليم بمكرهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The officials who saw signs of Joseph’s innocence nevertheless decided to imprison him for a time.
rows.anchor: ثم بدا لهم أي العزيز وأصحابه، في الرأي من بعد ما رأوا الآيات الدالة على براءة يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs of innocence included the shirt torn from behind, scratches to the face, and the women cutting their hands.
rows.anchor: وهي قد القميص من دبر وخمش في الوجه وتقطيع النسوة أيديهن

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the lām in the oath and in reported present-tense speech is used because both expressions carry the sense of speech and oath.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: هذه اللام في اليمين وفي كل مضارع القول

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says the phrase until a time means nine years.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: تسع سنين

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Joseph remained imprisoned five years.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: خمس سنين،

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the wife complained Joseph had publicly accused her of seducing him and asked either to leave to defend herself or for him to be imprisoned too.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: وذلك أن المرأة قالت لزوجها: إن هذا العبد العبراني قد فضحني في الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made prison a purification for Joseph’s desire toward the woman and an expiation for his lapse.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن الله تعالى جعل ذلك الحبس تطهيرا ليوسف من همته بالمرأة وتكفيرا لزلته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas counts three lapses by Joseph: the episode leading to prison, asking the cupbearer to remember him, and accusing his brothers of theft.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: عثر يوسف ثلاث عثرات: حين هم بها فسجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two prison newcomers were servants of King al-Akbar al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan: baker Majlath and cupbearer Banu; the king imprisoned them over an alleged poisoning plot.
rows.anchor: وهما غلامان كانا للملك الأكبر الوليد بن الريان، أحدهما خبازه صاحب طعامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says Egyptians bribed the two servants to poison the king’s food and drink; the cupbearer backed out, but the baker accepted the bribe and poisoned the food.
rows.anchor: ضمنوا لهما مالا ليسما طعام الملك وشرابه فأجاباهم إلى ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cupbearer warned the king not to eat, the baker warned him not to drink, and a test on an animal showed the food was poisoned, so both men were jailed.
rows.anchor: فقال الملك للساقي: اشرب فشربه فلم يضره، وقال للخباز: كل من طعامك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph had told prisoners he could interpret dreams; the two men approached to test him even though, Ibn Masʿud says, they had not actually dreamed anything.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن مسعود: ما رأى صاحبا يوسف شيئا، إنما كانا تحالفا أن يجربا علمه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas transmits a prophetic warning that whoever falsely claims to have seen a dream will be ordered to tie two barley grains together on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: من أرى عينيه في المنام ما لم تريا كلف أن يعقد بين شعرتين يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The same report warns that secretly listening to people who dislike it brings molten lead poured into the listener’s ear.
rows.anchor: ومن استمع لحديث قوم وهم له كارهون صب في أذنه الآنك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the two men loved Joseph at first sight; Joseph warned that those who loved him had each suffered a calamity, including his aunt, father, and the king’s wife.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: لما رأى الفتيان يوسف قالا له: والله لقد أحببناك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The cupbearer’s dream showed a grape seed bearing three clusters which he squeezed into the king’s cup and served him.
rows.anchor: فقال له الساقي: أيها العالم إني رأيت كأني غرست حبة من عنب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The baker’s dream showed three baskets of food above his head, eaten by birds; Ibn Masʿud’s reading clarifies the grape image as pressing grapes.
rows.anchor: وقال الخباز: إني رأيت كأن فوق رأسي ثلاث سلال فيها الخبز

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reads the cupbearer as saying he pressed grapes, making explicit that the word khamr here means grapes.
rows.anchor: ويدل عليه قراءة ابن مسعود أعصر عنبا

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi says an Arab called grapes he carried khamr, and vinegar made from grapes was also called wine-vinegar by association.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: أخبرني المعتمر أنه لقي أعرابيا معه عنب، فقال: ما معك؟ قال: خمر

rows.speaker: القتيبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybi allows literal wine by analogy with saying one pressed oil when olives were pressed.
rows.anchor: قال القتيبي: وقد تكون هي الخمر بعينها كما يقال: عصرت زيتا

rows.speaker: الفراء وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Farra and Ibn Ishaq say the prisoners call Joseph beneficent to them if he interprets their dreams; the phrase can be a polite appeal.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء وقال ابن إسحاق: إنا نراك من المحسنين إلينا إن فعلت ذلك

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says Joseph’s kindness in prison meant visiting the sick, making room for the cramped, gathering aid for the needy, and interceding for them.
rows.anchor: في قوله: إنا نراك من المحسنين ما كان إحسانه؟ قال كان إذا مرض رجل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Joseph treated sick prisoners, comforted the grieving, and devoted himself to his Lord.
rows.anchor: قتادة: بلغنا أن إحسانه كان يداوي مريضهم، ويعزي حزينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another story says Joseph encouraged hopeless inmates with promises of reward and cleansing; his kindness made the jailer let him choose any cell.
rows.anchor: فجعل يقول: أبشروا واصبروا تؤجروا، وإن لهذا لأجرا وثوابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph avoided immediately interpreting the dream because he knew one prisoner would suffer, and instead changed the subject.
rows.anchor: فكره يوسف (عليه السلام) أن يعبر لهما ما سألاه لما علم في ذلك من المكروه على أحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators understand Joseph’s promise to explain their food dreams before the food arrives as a claim to prophetic foreknowledge.
rows.anchor: هذا قول أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says he meant their ordinary waking food, telling them what it was, when they ate, and how much; they suspected divination, but he attributed knowledge to God.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أراد به في اليقظة فقال: لا يأتيكما طعام ترزقانه تطعمانه وتأكلانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated phrase that they are disbelievers in the Hereafter is analyzed as emphasis; another grammatical view treats the first pronoun as redundant and the second clause as the sentence.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم الأول جماد كقوله تعالى: أيعدكم أنكم إذا متم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text compares the grammatical redundancy with a Quranic construction in which the first clause is treated as omitted and the next begins anew.
rows.anchor: فصارت الأولى الملغاة والثانية ابتداء، وكافرون خبره

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud says the two prisoners admitted they had seen nothing and were only testing Joseph; Joseph replied that the matter had already been decreed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود: لما سمعا قول يوسف قالا: ما رأينا شيئا إنما كنا نلعب

rows.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي
rows.claim: Abu Ruzayn transmits the Prophet’s saying that a dream remains suspended until interpreted, is one forty-sixth of prophecy, and should be shared only with a person of judgment.
rows.anchor: قال: سمعت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول: «إن الرؤيا على رجل طائر ما لم تعبر

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas transmits a prophetic report that a dream is realized according to its first interpreter.
rows.anchor: عن أنس قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «الرؤيا لأول عابرة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators say Joseph thought the cupbearer would be saved; Qatada takes the thought as uncertain conjecture, but the author prefers the first as more fitting for prophets.
rows.anchor: هذا قول أكثر المفسرين، وفسره قتادة على الظن الذي هو خلاف اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him before his master, the king.
rows.anchor: اذكرني عند ربك سيدك يعني الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says Satan made Joseph forget his Lord, so he sought relief through a human and remained imprisoned longer; this was a lapse of heedlessness.
rows.anchor: فأنساه الشيطان ذكر ربه يعني أنسى الشيطان يوسف ذكر ربه عز وجل

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq instead takes the pronoun as referring to the cupbearer: Satan made him forget to mention Joseph to his master.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق: الهاء راجعة في قوله فأنساه الشيطان إلى الساقي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda defines biḍʿ as a number from three to five.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو عبيدة: هو ما بين الثلاثة إلى الخمسة

rows.speaker: مجاهد والأصمعي
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Asmaʿi define biḍʿ as three to nine.
rows.anchor: ومجاهد: ما بين الثلاث إلى التسع، الأصمعي: ما بين الثلاث إلى التسع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says biḍʿ is less than ten; al-Farra says Arabs use it from three through nine with tens, not with hundreds or thousands.
rows.anchor: وابن عباس: ما دون العشرة، وزعم الفراء أن البضع لا يذكر إلا مع العشرة والعشرين

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators say Joseph stayed seven years; Wahb compares his imprisonment with seven-year trials of Job and Nebuchadnezzar.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين على أن البضع في هذه الآية سبع سنين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan transmits the Prophet’s prayer for mercy on Joseph, saying his request to the cupbearer prolonged the imprisonment; al-Hasan weeps that people likewise turn to others in hardship.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «رحم الله يوسف، لولا كلمته ما لبث في السجن

rows.speaker: مالك بن دينار
rows.claim: Malik ibn Dinar says God rebuked Joseph for taking a human as an agent and lengthened his confinement after he asked the cupbearer to remember him.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك بن دينار: لما قال يوسف للساقي: اذكرني عند ربك، قيل له: يا يوسف اتخذت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a reported encounter, Gabriel tells Joseph that God asks why he sought help from human beings and swears to keep him in prison; Joseph accepts if God is pleased.
rows.anchor: قال له جبرئيل: يا طاهر الطاهرين، يقرأ عليك السلام رب العالمين ويقول: مالك؟ أما استحييت مني

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb recounts Gabriel asking Joseph who created, favored, accompanied in the well, rescued, and taught him; Joseph answers God each time and is asked why he appealed to a human.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب: قال جبرئيل ليوسف: إن الله تعالى يقول: من خلقك؟ قال: الله، قال: فمن حببك إلى أبيك

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the seven years of this imprisonment came after five earlier years; as release approached, the Egyptian king dreamed of seven fat cows consumed by seven lean ones.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي- وهذه السبعة سوى الخمسة التي كانت قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king also saw seven green ears and seven dry ones and summoned the elite to interpret the dream.
rows.anchor: وأرى سبع سنبلات خضر قد انعقد حبها وسبعا أخر يابسات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king’s advisers call the dream confused, frightening mixtures; aḍghāth literally means a bundle of vegetation, supported by a Quranic use and two poems.
rows.anchor: قالوا أضغاث أحلام أي أحلام مختلطة مشتبهة، أهاويل بأباطيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word aḥlām is the plural of ḥulm, dream, with the source noting its verb forms and morphology.
rows.anchor: والأحلام جمع الحلم وهو الرؤيا والفعل منه حلمت وأحلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surviving cupbearer remembered Joseph’s request after a long period and offered to interpret the dream; umma means a stretch of time.
rows.anchor: أي وتذكر حاجة يوسف قوله: اذكرني عند ربك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, and al-Dahhak read the phrase as after forgetfulness; Arabic also uses umma for forgetting.
rows.anchor: قراء ابن عباس وعكرمة والضحاك [بعد أمة] أي بعد نسيان

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda cites a poem using amihat to mean forgetting, supporting the lexical reading.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو عبيدة: أمهت وكنت لا أنسى حديثا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads amih with a still mīm and open initial vowel, another form for forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد: أمه، بسكون الميم وفتح الألف وهاء لخالصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cupbearer asks to be released and authorized to go to Joseph; the verse omits the intervening journey to prison.
rows.anchor: فأرسلون: فأطلقوني، وأذنوا لي أمضي وآتيكم بتأويله وفي الآية اختصار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Joseph’s prison was outside the city.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس لم يكن السجن في المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cupbearer addresses Joseph as al-ṣiddīq, meaning exceptionally truthful; Abu Bakr received the same title, and the form intensifies the quality.
rows.anchor: والصديق الكثير الصديق ولذلك سمي أبو بكر صديقا، وفعيل للمبالغة والكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph interprets the fat cows and green ears as seven fertile years and the lean cows and dry ears as years of severe drought.
rows.anchor: فقال لهم يوسف معلما ومعبرا: أما البقرات السمان والسنبلات الخضر فسبع سنين مخصبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dāʾban means the usual practice; another interpretation is industriously, and both dāʾban and dūʾban are valid forms for exerting effort.
rows.anchor: قرأ بعضهم دأبا بفتح الهمزة وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph tells them to leave harvested grain in its husk so it will keep and not spoil.
rows.anchor: فما حصدتم فذروه في سنبله في [بذره] إلا قليلا مما تأكلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven severe years of famine will consume most of the food stored during the fertile years, with only a little kept in reserve.
rows.anchor: ثم يأتي من بعد ذلك سبع شداد يعني سبع سنين جدد بالقحط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that years eat food is personification: as in poetry saying the day is heedless and night sleeps, people are heedless by day and sleep at night.
rows.anchor: يأكلن ما قدمتم لهن يعني يؤكل، فيهن ما أعددتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means they will preserve and store a little.
rows.anchor: إلا قليلا مما تحصنون أي: تخزنون وخزنون وتدخرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final favorable year was not in the king’s dream; God gave Joseph knowledge of an extra year, as Qatada says.
rows.anchor: وهذا خبر من يوسف (عليه السلام) عما لم يكن في رؤيا الملك، ولكنه من علم الغيب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God disclosed one additional year to Joseph beyond what the king asked him to interpret.
rows.anchor: كما قال قتادة: زاده الله علم سنة لم يسألوه عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yugāthu can mean people receive rain, or are relieved and aided; the rain is called ghayth.
rows.anchor: فيه يغاث الناس أي يمطرون بالغيث وهو المطر، وقيل: يغاثون

rows.speaker: أهل الكوفة
rows.claim: Kufa readers except Asim read taʿṣirūn in the second person because the surrounding speech addresses the people; others read yaʿṣirūn referring to them.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة إلا عاصما تعصرون، بالتاء لأن الكلام كله بالخطاب، وقرأ الباقون بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Most commentators say they will press grapes, olives, and sesame; Ibn Abbas instead says they will milk animals.
rows.anchor: وروى الفرج بن فضالة عن علي بن أبي طلحة عن ابن عباس قال: تعصرون تحلبون

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda takes yaʿṣirūn to mean escape drought and distress, since ʿaṣr can mean refuge; Abu Zubayd’s poem supports that sense.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: ينجون من الجدب والكرب، والعصر: المنجى والملجأ

rows.speaker: عيسى بن الأعرج
rows.claim: Isa ibn al-Aʿraj reads the verb passively, explaining that people will be rained upon; he links it with the rain from the clouds.
rows.anchor: يقرأها فيه يغاث الناس وفيه يعصرون، برفع الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the cupbearer relayed Joseph’s interpretation, the king realized it would come true and summoned its interpreter.
rows.anchor: لما رجع إلى الملك وأخبره بما أفتاه به يوسف من تأويل رؤياه كالنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph refused to leave prison with the messenger until his innocence was established, asking the king to investigate the women who cut their hands.
rows.anchor: أبى أن يخرج مع الرسول حتى يظهر عذره وبراءته

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: A transmission from Abu Bakr ibn Abbas says Asim read al-niswah with a rounded initial nūn.
rows.anchor: روى عبد الحميد بن صباح البرجمي ومحمد بن حبيب الشموني عن أبي بكر بن عباس عن عاصم قرأ النسوة بضم النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says God knows the women’s plotting; an alternative takes my lord as the Aziz, who knows Joseph is innocent of the accusation.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى بصنيعهن عالم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Joseph was brought out before the king had cleared the matter to his own satisfaction; the Aziz still suspected him of tempting his wife.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: فأخرج يوسف يومئذ قبل أن يسلم الملك لشأنه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet admires Joseph’s patience: he would have demanded release before interpreting the king’s dream and would have hurried out when summoned, while Joseph waited to clear his name.
rows.anchor: اشترط أن يخرجوني، ولقد عجبت من يوسف وكرمه وصبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage omits the messenger’s return and the king’s summoning of the women and Aziz’s wife before asking what happened when they solicited Joseph.
rows.anchor: فرجع الرسول إلى الملك من عند يوسف برسالة، فدعا الملك النسوة اللاتي قطعن أيديهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women say hāsha lillāh, meaning God forbid, and deny knowing any evil of Joseph; the Aziz’s wife confesses, and ḥaṣḥaṣ means truth became clear.
rows.anchor: فقال لهن: ما خطبكن: ما شأنكن وأمركن إذ راودتن يوسف عن نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ḥaṣḥaṣ is related to ḥaṣ, removing something completely; reduplicated forms such as kabkaba, kafkafa, and raddada are cited, with Abu Qays’s poem as evidence.
rows.anchor: والأصل فيه: حص وقيل: حصص، كما قيل: كبكبوا في كبوا، وكفكف في كف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife means that falsehood and lying have vanished and truth has appeared; she admits seduction and confirms Joseph’s honesty.
rows.anchor: ذهب الباطل والكذب وانقطع وتين الحق فظهر وبهر أنا راودته عن نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s ensuing words mean the Aziz should know Joseph did not betray him in his absence; the wife’s confession and Joseph’s statement are joined without naming the speaker transition.
rows.anchor: واتصل قول يوسف: ذلك ليعلم أني لم أخنه بالغيب بقول المرأة: أنا راودته عن نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares this abrupt linkage of different speakers with the queen’s words in 27:34 and Pharaoh’s words after his council in 26:35.
rows.anchor: وكذلك يفعلون بقول بلقيس: وجعلوا أعزة أهلها أذلة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra calls this an especially obscure construction: one person’s speech is narrated and another person’s statement follows without a fresh speaker attribution.
rows.anchor: روى أبو عبيدة عن الفراء أنه قال هذا من أغمض ما يأتي في الكلام
